newsitem.title: USA: High Court urged to uphold insider-trading law.
newsitem.headline: High Court urged to uphold insider-trading law.

text.p: A Justice Department lawyer urged the Supreme Court Wednesday to uphold one of the federal government's toughest enforcement weapons in fighting insider-trading abuses.

Deputy Solicitor General Michael Dreeben asked the high court to rule in favor of the government's interpretation of a section of the securities law that makes it a crime for a person to use confidential information in securities trading.

Under the theory, if an individual misappropriates secret information and trades on it, it is illegal because the person has breached a trust or duty, even if the individual is not a traditional company insider.

The arguments involved a U.S. appeals court ruling that overturned the conviction of James O'Hagan, a Minneapolis lawyer whose firm had been retained by London-based Grand Metropolitan Plc in connection with its 1988 takeover of Pillsbury Co.
He was convicted of using secret information about the deal to reap a $4.3 million profit in Pillsbury stock and stock options. O'Hagan was sentenced to 41 months in prison.
The U.S. Court of Appeals in St. Louis reversed his conviction last year on the grounds that he had not violated any fiduciary duty to Pillsbury stockholders.
But Dreeben argued that O'Hagan had breached a duty to his law firm, posing as a loyal partner while using confidential information entrusted to the firm to reap huge profits for his personal gain.

"Information is the lifeblood of the securities market. The deceptive acquisition and use of such information serves no legitimate purpose," he said. "Investors rely on the fact that the markets are essentially honest."

In reply to a question from Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, Dreeben admitted the law would not apply to someone who stole a lawyer's briefcase and traded on the information. He said that the thief would not breach any duty to the law firm.
"There are forms of improper conduct that section 10b (the provision of the law at issue) does not reach," he said.
"This is in essence a crime that involves surreptitious activities," Dreeben said. "This is a unique type of fraud, unique to the securities market."
The law has been used by the government in a number of high-profile cases against people who were not considered company insiders.

Those cases include a printer of secret tender offer documents, a psychiatrist who learned from a patient of a takeover bid and former Wall Street Journal reporter, R. Foster Winans, who leaked confidential information before it appeared in a widely read stocks column.

John French, a Minneapolis lawyer representing O'Hagan, said the law has "sown confusion." He said the conviction should have been overturned because "the relevant information was in the public domain" at the time of trades.

In any case, he said Congress since the 1980s has failed to clarify the reach of the law. "The Congress, if it wants to get the misappropriations theory into law, has to write it into law," he said. "Congress has not enacted it."
After the hour-long arguments, the Supreme Court took the case under advisement, with a ruling expected by July.
